questions.q: The minimum value of $\alpha$ for which the equation $\dfrac{4}{sinx} + \dfrac{1}{1 - sinx} = \alpha$ has at least one solution in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ is______.
questions.solution:
Let

$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{4}{sinx} + \dfrac{1}{1 - sinx}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{4}{sinx} + \dfrac{1 + sinx}{1 - \sin^{2}x}$

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = 4cosecx + {sec}^{2}x + tanxsecx$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{- 4cosx}{\sin^{2}x} + \dfrac{2sinx + 1}{\cos^{3}x} + \dfrac{\sin^{2}x}{\cos^{3}x}$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{- 4cosx}{\sin^{2}x} + \dfrac{{\left(sinx + 1\right)}^{2}}{\cos^{3}x}$

$⇒ {f}^{' '}\left(x\right) = - 4\left[\dfrac{- \sin^{3}x - 2sinx\cos^{2}x}{\sin^{4}x}\right] + \dfrac{2\left(sinx + 1\right)\cos^{4}x + 3\cos^{2}xsinx{\left(sinx + 1\right)}^{2}}{\cos^{6}x}$

$⇒ {f}^{' '}\left(x\right) = - 4\left[\dfrac{- \sin^{3}x - 2sinx\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)}{\sin^{4}x}\right] + \dfrac{2\left(sinx + 1\right){\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)}^{2} + 3\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)sinx{\left(sinx + 1\right)}^{2}}{{\left(1 - \sin^{2}x\right)}^{3}}$

For critical points,

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$

$⇒ \dfrac{{\left(sinx + 1\right)}^{2}}{\cos^{3}x} = \dfrac{4cosx}{\sin^{2}x}$

$⇒ \sin^{2}x{\left(sinx + 1\right)}^{2} = 4\cos^{4}x$

$⇒ sinx\left(sinx + 1\right) = 2\cos^{2}x$

$⇒ \sin^{2}x + sinx = 2 - 2\sin^{2}x$

$⇒ 3\sin^{2}x + sinx - 2 = 0$

$⇒ 3\sin^{2}x + 3sinx - 2sinx - 2 = 0$

$⇒ \left(3sinx - 2\right)\left(sinx + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ sinx = \dfrac{2}{3}$

Since, $sinx > 0 ∀ x \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

Now, at $sinx = \dfrac{2}{3}$, we get

$⇒ {f}^{' '}\left(x\right) = - 4\left[\dfrac{- \dfrac{8}{27} - \dfrac{4}{3}\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{9}\right)}{\dfrac{16}{81}}\right] + \dfrac{2 \times \dfrac{5}{3}{\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{9}\right)}^{2} + 3\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{9}\right) \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{25}{9}}{{\left(1 - \dfrac{4}{9}\right)}^{3}}$

$⇒ {f}^{' '}\left(x\right) = \left[4\left[\dfrac{28}{27} \times \dfrac{81}{16}\right] + \dfrac{2 \times \dfrac{5}{3}{\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right)}^{2} + 3\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right) \times \dfrac{2}{3} \times \dfrac{25}{9}}{{\left(\dfrac{5}{9}\right)}^{3}}\right] > 0$

Hence, it is the point of minima.

$∴ f{\left(x\right)}_{min} = \dfrac{4}{\dfrac{2}{3}} + \dfrac{1}{1 - \dfrac{2}{3}} = 9$

$f{\left(x\right)}_{max} \to \infty$

$f\left(x\right)$ is continuous function

$∴ {\alpha}_{min} = 9$

questions.q: The position of a moving car at time $t$ is given by $f ( t ) = a{t}^{2} + bt + c, t > 0$, where $a, b\text{and}c$ are real numbers greater than $1$. Then the average speed of the car over the time interval $\left[{t}_{1}, {t}_{2}\right]$ is attained at the point:
questions.solution:
Given: position of the moving car at time $t\text{is} = f\left(t\right) = a{t}^{2} + bt + c$

So,

${v}_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{f\left({t}_{2}\right) - f\left({t}_{1}\right)}{{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}$

$⇒ {v}_{\text{avg}} = \dfrac{a\left({t}_{2}^{2} - {t}_{1}^{2}\right) + b\left({t}_{2} - {t}_{1}\right)}{{t}_{2} - {t}_{1}}$

$⇒ {v}_{\text{avg}} = a\left({t}_{1} + {t}_{2}\right) + b$

The instantaneous speed is given by:

${f}^{'}\left(t\right) = 2at + b$

So, to get the point where average speed is equal to car's actual speed,

${f}^{'}\left(t\right) = {v}_{\text{avg}}$

$⇒ a\left({t}_{1} + {t}_{2}\right) + b = at + b$

$⇒ t = \dfrac{{t}_{1} + {t}_{2}}{2}$

questions.q: Suppose $f\left(x\right)$ is a polynomial of degree four having critical points at $- 1, 0, 1$. If $T = \left\{x \in R | f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right)\right\}$, then the sum of squares of all the elements of $T$ is :
questions.solution:
${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = k . x\left(x + 1\right)\left(x - 1\right)$

$= k\left({x}^{3} - x\right)$

Integrating both sides with respect to $x$, we get

$f\left(x\right) = k\left(\dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) + c$

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = c$

$∵ f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right)$

$⇒ k\dfrac{\left({x}^{4} - 2{x}^{2}\right)}{4} + c = c$

$⇒ {x}^{2}\left({x}^{2} - 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ x = 0, \sqrt{2}, - \sqrt{2}$

$⇒ T = \left\{0, \sqrt{2}, - \sqrt{2}\right\}$

Thus, sum of squares of all the elements of $T$ is ${\left(0\right)}^{2} + {\left(\sqrt{2}\right)}^{2} + {\left(- \sqrt{2}\right)}^{2} = 4$.

Surface area of cube $\left(s\right) = 6{a}^{2}$

$⇒ 12\left(10\right)\dfrac{da}{dt} = 3 . 6 ⇒ \dfrac{da}{dt} = 0 . 03cm / sec$

Now, volume of cube $\left(V\right) = {a}^{3}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dv}{dt} = 3{a}^{2 .}\dfrac{da}{dt} = 3 ( 10{)}^{2}\left(0 . 03\right) = 9c{m}^{3} / sec$

questions.solution:
For the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4x$, $a = 1$

Let $\left(a{t}^{2}, 2at\right) = \left(1, 2\right)

$⇒ t = 1$

So, equation of normal is $tx + y = 2at + a{t}^{3}$.

$⇒ x + y = 3$ intersects $x -$axis at \left(3, 0\right)

Given curve $y = {e}^{x} ⇒ $\dfrac{dy}{dx} =${e}^{x}

So, equation of $tangent to the curve at \left(c, {e}^{c}\right) is$y - {e}^{c} = {e}^{c}$\left(x - c\right)$.

At $\left(3, 0\right) ⇒ 0 - {e}^{c} = {e}^{c}\left(3 - c\right) ⇒ c = 4$.

$| b - a | = 1$

If general equation of circle is ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ then its center is $\left(- g, - f\right)$ and radius is $\sqrt{{g}^{2} + {f}^{2} - c}$

Two circles touches each other if ${C}_{1}{C}_{2} = \left|{r}_{1} \pm {r}_{2}\right|

Distance between ${C}_{2}$\left(3, 0\right)and{C}_{1}\left(0, 4\right) is either $\sqrt{k} + 1or$\left|\sqrt{k} - 1\right|$

${C}_{1}{C}_{2} = \sqrt{{\left(3 - 0\right)}^{2} + {\left(0 - 4\right)}^{2}} = 5$

$⇒ \sqrt{k} + 1 = 5$or $\left|\sqrt{k} + 1\right| = 5$

$⇒ k = 16 or k = 36$

$⇒$ Maximum value of $k$ is $36$.

Given, $F\left(x\right) = {∫}_{1}^{x}{t}^{2}g\left(t\right)dt$

$⇒ {F}^{''}\left(1\right) = 0 + 1 \times 3$

$⇒ {F}^{''}\left(1\right) = 3$

${F}^{'}\left(x\right) = {x}^{2}g\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {F}^{'}\left(1\right) = 1 . g\left(1\right) = 0$\left(∵ g\left(1\right) = 0\right)$

Now ${F}^{''}\left(x\right) = 2xg\left(x\right) + {x}^{2}{g}^{'}\left(x\right)$

$⇒ {F}^{''}\left(x\right) = 2xg\left(x\right) + {x}^{2}f\left(x\right)$\left(∵ {g}^{'}\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right)\right)$

$⇒ {F}^{''}\left(1\right) = 0 + 1 \times 3$

$⇒ {F}^{''}\left(1\right) = 3$

$F\left(x\right)$ has a local minimum at $x = 1$.

questions.q: The length of the perpendicular from the origin, on normal to the curve, ${x}^{2} + 2xy - 3{y}^{2} = 0$, at the point $\left(2, 2\right)$, is.
questions.solution:
${x}^{2} + 2xy - 3{y}^{2} = 0$

Differentiate the above curve,

$2x + 2\left[xy ' + y\right] - 6yy ' = 0$

So, at $\left(2, 2\right), y ' = 1$.

So, equation of normal to the curve at $\left(2, 2\right)$ is $x + y = 4$.

Thus, perpendicular distance from origin on the normal is

$\left|\dfrac{0 + 0 - 4}{\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2}}}\right|$

$= \left|\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{2}}\right| = 2\sqrt{2}$.

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = x\cos^{- 1} ⁡ \left(- sin ⁡ \left|x\right|\right), x \in \left[- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right],$ then which of the following is true?
options: $f'$ is increasing in $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$ and decreasing in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
$f'$ is decreasing in $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, 0\right)$ and increasing in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$
questions.solution:
${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = x\left(\pi - \cos^{- 1}\left(sin\left|x\right|\right)\right) = x ( \pi\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \sin^{- 1}\left(sin\left|x\right|\right)\right) = x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + \left|x\right|\right)$
$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} + x\right) & x \ge 0 \\ x\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - x\right) & x < 0\end{cases}\right$
${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\dfrac{\pi}{2} + 2x & x \ge 0 \\ \dfrac{\pi}{2} - 2x & x < 0\end{cases}\right$
${f}^{'}\left(x\right)$ is increasing in $\left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and decreasing in $\left(\dfrac{- \pi}{2}, 0\right)$.

questions.solution:
As $f\left(x\right)$, is polynomial function, so it is continuous and differentiable in $\left[0,1\right]$.

Here $f\left(0\right) = 11$, $f\left(1\right) = 1 - 4 + 8 + 11 = 16$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 3{x}^{2} - 8x + 8$

$∴ {f}^{.}\left(c\right) = \dfrac{f\left(1\right) - f\left(0\right)}{1 - 0} = \dfrac{16 - 11}{1} = 3{c}^{2} - 8c + 8$

$3{c}^{2} - 8c + 3 = 0$

$c = \dfrac{8 \pm 2\sqrt{7}}{6} = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{7}}{3}$

$∴ c = \dfrac{4 - \sqrt{7}}{3} \in \left(0,1\right)$.

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right)$ be a polynomial of degree $5$ such that $x = \pm 1$ are its critical points. If $\lim_{x \to 0}\left(2 + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{{x}^{3}}\right) = 4,$ then which one of the following is not true?
options: $f\left(1\right) - 4f\left(- 1\right) = 4$ . $x = 1$ is a point of maximum and $x = - 1$
$x = 1$is a point of local minimum and $x = - 1$ is a point of local maximum
$x = 1$ is a point of local maxima of $f$
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = a{x}^{5} + b{x}^{4} + c{x}^{3}$

Consider, $\lim_{x \to 0} ⁡ \left(2 + \dfrac{a{x}^{5} + b{x}^{4} + c{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}\right) = 4$

$⇒ 2 + c = 4$

$⇒ c = 2$

Differentiating $f\left(x\right)$ with respect to $x$

${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 5a{x}^{4} + 4b{x}^{3} + 6{x}^{2}$

$= {x}^{2}\left(5a{x}^{2} + 4bx + 6\right)$

Critical points of the function are given as $\pm 1$.

${f}^{'}\left(1\right) = 0 ⇒ 5a + 4b + 6 = 0$

${f}^{'}\left(- 1\right) = 0 ⇒ 5a - 4b + 6 = 0$
Solving both we get, $b = 0$, $a = - \dfrac{6}{5}$
So, $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{- 6}{5}{x}^{5} + 2{x}^{3}$
And ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = - 6{x}^{4} + 6{x}^{2}$

$= - 6{x}^{2}\left(x + 1\right)\left(x - 1\right)$

Hence, local minima at $x = - 1$ and local maxima at $x = 1$.

Hence $( m, M ) = ( 4, 3\sqrt{3} )$

questions.q: If the tangent to the curve $y = \dfrac{x}{{x}^{2} - 3}, x \in R, \left(x \ne \pm \sqrt{3}\right),$ at a point $\left(\alpha, \beta\right) \ne \left(0, 0\right)$ on it is parallel to the line $2x + 6y - 11 = 0,$ then:
questions.solution:
The slope of a line $ax + by + c = 0$ is $- \dfrac{a}{b},$ hence the slope of the given line $2x + 6y - 11 = 0$ is $- \dfrac{1}{3} .

Also, we know that$ the slope of tangent to a curvey = f $\left(x\right)$ at a point $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ is ${\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)}$

We have $y = \dfrac{x}{{x}^{2} - 3}$

Applying quotient rule for differentiation, i.e. $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right) = \dfrac{v \cdot \left(\dfrac{du}{dx}\right) - u \cdot \left(\dfrac{dv}{dx}\right)}{{u}^{2}},$ we get

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1 \cdot \left({x}^{2} - 3\right) - x \cdot 2x}{{\left({x}^{2} - 3\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{{x}^{2} - 3 - 2{x}^{2}}{{\left({x}^{2} - 3\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = - \dfrac{{x}^{2} + 3}{{\left({x}^{2} - 3\right)}^{2}}$

Also, we have $⇒ {\left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)}_{\left(\alpha, \beta\right)} = - \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ - \dfrac{{\alpha}^{2} + 3}{{\left({\alpha}^{2} - 3\right)}^{2}} = - \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ 3{\alpha}^{2} + 9 = {\left({\alpha}^{2} - 3\right)}^{2}$

$⇒ 3{\alpha}^{2} + 9 = {\alpha}^{4} - 6{\alpha}^{2} + 9$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{4} - 9{\alpha}^{2} = 0$

$⇒ {\alpha}^{2}\left({\alpha}^{2} - 9\right) = 0$

$⇒ \alpha = 0, 3, - 3$

But $\alpha \ne 0, ⇒ \alpha = 3, - 3$

For $\alpha = 3, \beta = \dfrac{3}{{3}^{2} - 3} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \left|6\alpha + 2\beta\right| = 19$ and $\left|2\alpha + 6\beta\right| = 9$

For $\alpha = - 3, \beta = - \dfrac{3}{6} = - \dfrac{1}{2}$

$⇒ \left|6\alpha + 2\beta\right| = 19$ and $\left|2\alpha + 6\beta\right| = 9 .

$

questions.q: A spherical iron ball of radius $10cm$ is coated with a layer of ice of uniform thickness that melts at a rate of $50c{m}^{3} / min .$ When the thickness of the ice is $5cm,$ then the rate at which the thickness $($in $cm / min )$ of the ice decreases, is :
questions.solution:
We know that the volume of a sphere of radius $r$ is $\dfrac{4}{3}{\pi r}^{3} .$

Given the radius of the spherical iron ball is $R = 10cm$ and the thickness of the ice is $xcm .$


Volume of ice: $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{\left(R + x\right)}^{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{R}^{3}$

$⇒ V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{\left(10 + x\right)}^{3} - \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{\left(10\right)}^{3}$

Differentiating with respect to $t,$ we get

$\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi{\left(10 + x\right)}^{2}\dfrac{dx}{dt} - 0$

Given $\dfrac{dV}{dt} = 50c{m}^{3} / min$

$⇒ 50 = 4\pi{\left(10 + x\right)}^{2}\dfrac{dx}{dt}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dx}{dt} = \dfrac{50}{4\pi{\left(10 + x\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ {\left\dfrac{dx}{dt}\right|}_{x = 5} = \dfrac{50}{4\pi{\left(15\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{18\pi}cm / min .$

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = {e}^{x} - x$ and $g\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} - x, ∀ xϵR$ . Then the set of all $xϵR$ , where the function $h\left(x\right) = \left(fog\right)\left(x\right)$ is increasing, is:
questions.solution:
$h\left(x\right) = fog\left(x\right) = {e}^{g\left(x\right)} - g\left(x\right)$
$= {e}^{{x}^{2} - x} - \left({x}^{2} - x\right)$
${h}^{'}\left(x\right) = {e}^{{x}^{2} - x} \times \left(2x - 1\right) - 2x + 1$
$= \left(2x - 1\right)\left({e}^{{x}^{2} - x} - 1\right)$
$∵ h\left(x\right)$ is increasing $∴ {h}^{'}\left(x\right) \ge 0$⇒ \left(2x - 1\right)\left({e}^{{x}^{2} - x} - 1\right) \ge 0$
Case 1: $\left(2x - 1\right) \ge 0$ & ${x}^{2} - x \ge 0$
$⇒ x \ge \dfrac{1}{2} \text{ and } x \in \left(- \infty, 0\right] ∪ \left[1, \infty\right) ⇒ x \in \left[1, \infty\right)$
Case 2: $\left(2x - 1\right) \le 0$ and ${x}^{2} - x \le 0$
$x < \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $x \in \left(0, 1\right)$⇒ x \in \left(0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right]$
$∴ x \in \left[0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right] ∪ [ 1, \infty )$

questions.q: A water tank has the shape of an inverted right circular cone, whose semi-vertical angle is $\tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) .$ Water is poured into it at a constant rate of $5cubicm / min .$ Then the rate $($in $m / min ) ,$ at which the level of water is rising at the instant when the depth of water in the tank is $10m;$ is:
questions.solution:
The given water tank is of the shape shown by the diagram.

The semi-vertical angle $\theta = \tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right), ⇒ tan\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Let at any time $tmin,$ height of water level is $hm$ and radius of cone filled with water be $rm .

Also, we have $tan\theta = $\dfrac{r}{h}

$⇒ $\dfrac{r}{h} = \dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ r = $\dfrac{h}{2}$ . . . $\left(i\right)$

Now, the volume of the water at time $tmin$ in the cone is $V = \dfrac{1}{3}$\pi{r}^{2}h$

On putting the value of $r from $the equation \left(i\right),$ we get

$V = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\left(\dfrac{{h}^{3}}{4}\right)$ = $\dfrac{\pi}{12}\left({h}^{3}\right)

Now, differentiating$ with respect tot,$ we get

\dfrac{dV}{dt} = \dfrac{\pi}{12} ⋅ \left(3{h}^{2}\dfrac{dh}{dt}\right)

Put the given value of \dfrac{dV}{dt} \text{$ and } h$

$⇒ 5 =$\dfrac{\pi}{4}$⋅ $\left(100\dfrac{dh}{dt}\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{dh}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{5\pi}m / min$

questions.q: If $f ( x )$ is a non-zero polynomial of degree four, having local extreme points at $x = – 1, 0, 1;$ then the set $S = { x \in R: f\left(x\right) = f\left(0\right) }$ contains exactly
options: Two irrational and two rational numbers
Two irrational and one rational number
questions.solution:
$f ( x )$ has extreme points at ${ - 1, 0, 1 }$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$ at $x = – 1, 0, 1$

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = a\left({x}^{2} - 1\right)x ∵ f\left(x\right)$ is a polynomial

$⇒ f\left(x\right) = ∫ a\left({x}^{3} - x\right)dx = a\left(\dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) + C$

Now the equation,

$f\left(x\right) = f ( 0 )$

$⇒ a\left(\dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2}\right) + C = C$
$⇒ \dfrac{{x}^{4}}{4} - \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{2} = 0 ⇒ {x}^{2}\left({x}^{2} - 2\right) = 0$
$⇒ x = 0, \pm \sqrt{2}$

$⇒ S = { 0, \sqrt{2}, - \sqrt{2} } .$

Hence, the set contains two irrational and one rational number.

questions.q: If the tangent to the curve, $y = {x}^{3} + ax – b$ at the point $( 1, – 5 )$ is perpendicular to the line, $– x + y + 4 = 0,$ then which one of the following points lies on the curve?
questions.solution:
Given $y = {x}^{3} + ax - b$

$∵$ it passes through $\left(1, - 5\right)$

$∴ 1 + a - b = - 5$

$⇒ a - b = - 6 . . . \left(1\right)

Slope$ of the lineax + by + c = 0$ is $- $\dfrac{a}{b}$,$ hence, slope of the line $- x + y + 4 = 0$ is $1$

We know that if two lines are perpendicular, then the product of their slopes is $- 1 .

$∴$ Slope of tangent of $y,$ which is perpendicular to $- x + y + 4 = 0$ is $- 1$

Also, we know that the slop of tangent to a curve $y = f \left(x\right) at a point \left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) is given by ${f}^{'}$\left({x}_{1}\right)$ .

$∴ {f}^{'}\left(1\right) = - 1$

And, ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 3{x}^{2} + a$

$⇒ 3 + a = - 1$

$⇒ a = - 4 . . . \left(2\right)$

From $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(2\right),$ we get $a = - 4, b = 2$

$∴ f\left(x\right) = y = {x}^{3} - 4x - 2$

At, $x = 2, y = {2}^{3} - 4 \times 2 - 2 = - 2$ and at $x = - 2, y = {\left(- 2\right)}^{3} - 4 \times 2 - 2 = - 18 .

Thus, out of the given options only \left(2, - 2\right) satisfy the curve, hence this point will lie on the curve.

$

questions.q: Let $S$ be the set of all values of $x$ for which the tangent to the curve $y = f\left(x\right) = {x}^{3} - {x}^{2} - 2x$ at $( x, y )$ is parallel to the line segment joining the points $( 1, f ( 1 ) ) and \left(- 1, f\left(- 1\right)\right),$ then $S$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $y = f\left(x\right) = {x}^{3} - {x}^{2} - 2x$

$⇒ f\left(1\right) = 1 - 1 - 2 = - 2$

$⇒ f\left(- 1\right) = - 1 - 1 + 2 = 0$

The slope of a line joining the points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) \text{ and } \left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is $\dfrac{{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}}{{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}}$

Thus, the slope of the line segment joining the points $\left(1, f\left(1\right)$\right) $\text{$ and } $\left(- 1, f \left(- 1\right)\right)$ is $m = \dfrac{f ( 1 ) - f \left(- 1\right)}{1 + 1} = \dfrac{- 2 - 0}{2} =- 1$

Given, this line segment is parallel to the tangent of the curve $y = f \left(x\right),$ at $\left(x, y\right)$ and we know that the slope of the tangent to $y = f \left(x\right) is \dfrac{dy}{dx}$,$ also the slope of two parallel lines is same, hence

$m = $\dfrac{dy}{dx} =$ 3{x}^{2} - 2x - 2$

$⇒ 3{x}^{2} - 2x - 2 = - 1$

$⇒ 3{x}^{2} - 2x - 1 = 0$

$⇒ $\left(x - 1\right) \left(3x + 1\right)$ = 0$

$⇒ x = 1, $- \dfrac{1}{3}$ .

Hence,$ the setS$ is $\left\{- \dfrac{1}{3}, 1\right\}$ .

questions.q: The height of a right circular cylinder of maximum volume inscribed in a sphere of radius $3$ is:
questions.solution:
From the diagram, we get radius of cylinder $= \sqrt{{R}^{2} - {\left(\dfrac{h}{2}\right)}^{2}}$
$⇒$ Volume of cylinder $V = \pi\left({R}^{2} - \dfrac{{h}^{2}}{4}\right)h$

$⇒ {h}^{2} = \dfrac{4{R}^{2}}{3} = \dfrac{4 \times 9}{3} = 12$
$⇒ h = 2\sqrt{3}$

questions.q: Given that the slope of the tangent to a curve $y = y ( x )$ at any point $\left(x, y\right)$ is $\dfrac{2y}{{x}^{2}}$. If the curve passes through the centre of the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} - 2x - 2y = 0,$ then its equation is
questions.solution:
Slope of tangent, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{2y}{{x}^{2}}$

Integrating both sides, we get,
$ln ⁡ y = - \dfrac{2}{x} + c$
$∵$ it passes through centre $\left(1, 1\right)$ of given circle,

questions.solution:
Equation of line parallel to given line can be taken as

$y = 2x + c$.

Now, this line touches the curve $y = {x}^{2} - 5x + 5$ hence, roots of the equation

${x}^{2} - 5x + 5 = 2x + c ⇒ {x}^{2} - 7x + \left(5 - c\right) = 0$ must be equal.

$⇒ D = 0 ⇒ {\left(- 7\right)}^{2} - 4 \cdot 1 \cdot \left(5 - c\right) = 0 ⇒ 4c = - 29$

Hence, equation of tangent is $4y = 8x - 29$.

Clearly, it passes through $\left(\dfrac{1}{8}, - 7\right)$.

questions.q: The maximum area (in sq. units) of a rectangle having its base on the $x -$ axis and its other two vertices on the parabola, $y = 12 - {x}^{2}$ such that the rectangle lies inside the parabola, is :
questions.solution:
Since, given parabola is symmetric about the $y -$ axis, hence rectangle will also be symmetric about $y -$ axis.

Let one vertex of the rectangle on the $x -$ axis be $\left(\alpha, 0\right), then

Area$ of rectangle A = 2\alpha .$\left(12 - {\alpha}^{2}\right)$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $\alpha$, we get

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{d\alpha} = 24 - 6{\alpha}^{2} = 0 ⇒ \alpha = 2, - 2$

For area to be maximum, put $\alpha = 2$ in the equation for area of the rectangle, we get

${A}_{max} = 2 \times 2 \times \left(12 - {2}^{2}\right) = 32$

questions.solution:
$f(x)=\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}-\frac{(d-x)}{\sqrt{b^{2}+(d-x)^{2}}}$=\frac{x}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}+\frac{(x-d)}{\sqrt{b^{2}+(x-d)^{2}}}$\begin{array}{l}

\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)>0, \square x \in R

questions.q: A helicopter is flying along the curve given by $y - x\dfrac{3}{2} = 7, \left(x \ge 0\right) .$ A soldier positioned at the point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 7\right)$, who wants to shoot down the helicopter when it is nearest to him. Then this nearest distance is:
questions.solution:
We have

$y = 7 + {x}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{x}$

Let the point on curve be $P\left({x}_{1}, 7 + {x}_{1}^${$\dfrac{3}{2}$}$\right)$ and given point beA$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, 7\right)$.

For nearest point normal at $P$ passes through $A$.

So, the slope of line $AP =$ Slope of normal at $P$

$⇒ {x}_{1}^{\dfrac{3}{2}}{x}_{1} - \dfrac{1}{2} = {{\left- \dfrac{dx}{dy}\right|}_{\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)}}_{} = - \dfrac{2}{3\sqrt{{x}_{1}}}$

$⇒ 3{x}_{1}^{2} = 1 - 2{x}_{1}$

$⇒ 3{x}_{1}^{2} + 2{x}_{1} - 1 = 0$

$⇒ \left({x}_{1} + 1\right)\left(3{x}_{1} - 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ {x}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{3} ( {x}_{1} = - 1$, is not possible as ${x}_{1} > 0 )$

Hence, point $P$ is $\left(\dfrac{1}{3}, 7 + \dfrac{1}{3\sqrt{3}}\right)$.

So, $AP = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{36} + \dfrac{1}{27}} = \dfrac{1}{6}\sqrt{\dfrac{7}{3}}$ units.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The shortest distance between the point $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right)$ and the curve $y = \sqrt{x}, \left(x > 0\right) , is$
questions.solution:
Let $P$ be the nearest to $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right),$ then normal at $P$ will pass through $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right) .$

Any point on the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4ax$ can be taken as $\left(a{t}^{2}, 2at\right)$

Let, co-ordinates of $P$ on the curve $y = \sqrt{x}, ⇒ {y}^{2} = x$ can be taken as $\left(\dfrac{{t}^{2}}{4}, \dfrac{t}{2}\right)$


The equation of the normal to the parabola ${y}^{2} = 4ax$ at a point $\left(a{t}^{2}, 2at\right)$ is $y + tx = 2at + a{t}^{3} .$

Hence, the equation of normal to $y = \sqrt{x}$ or ${y}^{2} = x$ at $\left(\dfrac{{t}^{2}}{4}, \dfrac{t}{2}\right)$ is $y + tx = \dfrac{t}{2} + \dfrac{{t}^{3}}{4}$

This line passes through $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right),$ hence
$\dfrac{3t}{2} = \dfrac{t}{2} + \dfrac{{t}^{3}}{4}$

$⇒ {t}^{3} - 4t = 0$

$⇒ t\left({t}^{2} - 4\right) = 0$

$⇒ t = 0, 2, - 2$ but $- 2$ is rejected as we have to take point in the first quadrant.

Thus, the points are $\left(0, 0\right)$ or $\left(1, 1\right)$ and the distances of these points from $\left(\dfrac{3}{2}, 0\right)$ are respectively

$\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{3}{2} - 0\right)}^{2} + {\left(0 - 0\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$ and $\sqrt{{\left(\dfrac{3}{2} - 1\right)}^{2} + {\left(1 - 0\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ units.

Hence, nearest point is $\left(1, 1\right)$ and the minimum distance is $\dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{2}$ units.

questions.q: The maximum volume $\left(incu . m\right)$ of the right circular cone having slant height $3m$ is:
questions.solution:
Given $l = 3$



$⇒ {r}^{2} + {h}^{2} = {l}^{2} = 9$

Volume, $V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi{r}^{2}h$

$⇒ V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(9 - {h}^{2}\right)h = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(9h - {h}^{3}\right)$

$\dfrac{dv}{dh} = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(9 - 3{h}^{2}\right)$

$\dfrac{dv}{dh} = 0 ⇒ h = \sqrt{3}$

$\dfrac{{d}^{2}V}{d{h}^{2}} = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi\left(- 6h\right) < 0$

questions.q: Let $M$ and $m$ be respectively the absolute maximum and the absolute minimum values of the function, $f\left(x\right) = 2{x}^{3} - 9{x}^{2} + 12x + 5$ in the interval $[ 0, 3 ]$ . Then $M - m$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given $f\left(x\right) = 2{x}^{3} - 9{x}^{2} + 12x + 5, x \in \left[0, 3\right]$

Differentiating w.r.t $x$,

$⇒ {f}^{′}\left(x\right) = 6{x}^{2} - 18x + 12$

$⇒ {f}^{′}\left(x\right) = 6\left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right)$

For maxima/minima ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$

$⇒ 6\left(x - 1\right)\left(x - 2\right) = 0 ⇒ x = 1, 2$

Now, ${f}^{"}\left(x\right) = 12x - 18$

So at $x = 1, {f}^{"}\left(x\right) < 0$

and at $x = 2, {f}^{"}\left(x\right) > 0$

So, for absolute maxima/minima

$⇒ f\left(1\right) = 10$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = 9$

$⇒ f\left(0\right) = 5$

$⇒ f\left(3\right) = 14$

$⇒ M = 14$

$⇒ m = 5$

$∴$M - m = 9$

questions.q:
Let $f(x)$ be a polynomial of degree 4 having extreme values at $x=1$ and $x=2$.
If $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{f(x)}{x^2}+1\right)=3$ then $f(-1)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\because f(x)$ has extremum values at x=1 and $x=2\because f^{\prime}(1)=0 and f^{\prime}(2)=0$
As, $f(x)$ is a polynomial of degree 4 .
Suppose $f(x)=A x^4+B x^3+C x^2+D x+E \begin{aligned}$&\because $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{f(x)}{x^2}+$1\right)=3 \\
&\Rightarrow $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(\frac{A x^4+B x^3+C x^2+D x+E}{x^2}+$1\right)=3 \\
&\Rightarrow $\lim _{x \rightarrow 0}\left(A x²+B x+C+\frac{D}{x}+\frac{E}{x^2}$+$1\right)=3
\end{aligned}

As limit has finite value, so $D=0 and E=0$
Now A(0)^2+B(0)+C+0+0+1=3 \begin{aligned}$&\Rightarrow c+1=3 \Rightarrow c=2 \\
&f^{\prime}(x)=4 A x³+3 B x²+2 C x+D \\
&f^{\prime}(1)=0 \Rightarrow 4 A(1)+3 B(1)+2 C(1)+D=0
\end{aligned}

$\begin{aligned}$& \Rightarrow 4 A+3 B=-4 \\
f^{\prime}(2)=0 & \Rightarrow 4 A(8)+3 B(4)+2 C(2)+D=0 \\
& \Rightarrow 8 A+3 B=-2
\end{aligned} From $equations (1) and (2), we getA=\frac{1}{2} and B=-2$
So, $f(x)=\frac{x^4}{2}-2 x^3+2 x^2$
Therefore, $f(-1)=\frac{(-1)^4}{2}-2(-1)^3+2(-1)^2$
=$\frac{1}{2}+$2+2=$\frac{9}{2}Hence $f(-1)=$\frac{9}{2}$

questions.q: If a right circular cone, having maximum volume, is inscribed in a sphere of radius $3cm$, then the curved surface area (in ${cm}^{2}$) of this cone is :
questions.solution:
In $△ AMC, AM = 3sin2\theta \text{ and } MC = 3cos2\theta$

$V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi{r}^{2}h$ where, $r$ is radius and $h$ is height of cone

$⇒ V = \dfrac{1}{3}\pi{\left(3sin ⁡ 2\theta\right)}^{2}\left(3 + 3cos2\theta\right)$

(since, radius of cone $= AM$ and height of cone $= MC$)

$⇒ V = \pi\left(36\sin^{2} ⁡ \theta\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta\right)\left(2\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta\right)\left[∵ sin ⁡ 2\theta = 2sin ⁡ \thetacos ⁡ \theta \text{ and } cos ⁡ 2\theta = 2\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta - 1\right]$

$= 72\pi\sin^{2} ⁡ \theta\cos^{4} ⁡ \theta$

Differentiating both sides with respect to $\theta$, we get

$\dfrac{dv}{d\theta} = 72\pi\left[2sin ⁡ \theta\cos^{5} ⁡ \theta - 4\sin^{3} ⁡ \theta\cos^{3} ⁡ \theta\right]$

For maximum value, $\dfrac{dV}{d\theta} = 0$

$⇒ 72\pi\left[2sin ⁡ \theta\cos^{5} ⁡ \theta - 4\sin^{3} ⁡ \theta\cos^{3} ⁡ \theta\right] = 0 ⇒ \tan^{2} ⁡ \theta = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Thus, volume is maximum when $tan ⁡ \theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$

Hence, curved surface area $S = \pirl$

$= \pir\sqrt{{\left(3 + 3cos ⁡ 2\theta\right)}^{2} + {( 3sin ⁡ 2\theta )}^{2}}\left[∵ l = \sqrt{{r}^{2} + {h}^{2}}\right]$

$= \pi\left(3sin ⁡ 2\theta\right)\sqrt{36\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta} = 18\pi\left(2sin ⁡ \theta\cos^{2} ⁡ \theta\right)$

$= 36\pi\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} . \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{24\pi}{\sqrt{3}} = 8\sqrt{3}\pi$

questions.q: If the curves ${y}^{2} = 6x, 9{x}^{2} + b{y}^{2} = 16$ intersect each other at right angles, then the value of $b$ is:
questions.solution:
Given, curves ${y}^{2} = 6x and 9{x}^{2} + b{y}^{2} = 16$
Let the point of intersection of curves be $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right) .$ So,
$2{y}_{1}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 6$
$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{3}{{y}_{1}}$
$18{x}_{1} + 2b{y}_{1}\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 0$
$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{- 9{x}_{1}}{b{y}_{1}}$

Since both the curve intersect at right angle.

$\left(\dfrac{3}{{y}_{1}}\right) \times \left(\dfrac{- 9{x}_{1}}{b{y}_{1}}\right) = - 1$

$⇒ 27{x}_{1} = b{y}_{1}^{2}$ (Since ${y}_{1}^{2} = 6{x}_{1}$)

$⇒ 27{x}_{1} = b\left(6{x}_{1}\right)$

${x}_{1} \ne 0$

$b = \dfrac{27}{6} = \dfrac{9}{2}$

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{x}^{2}}$ and $g\left(x\right) = x - \dfrac{1}{x}, x \in R - \left\{- 1, 0, 1\right\} .$ If $h\left(x\right) = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{g\left(x\right)}$ , then the local minimum value of $h\left(x\right)$ is:
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} + \dfrac{1}{{x}^{2}} = {\left(x - \dfrac{1}{x}\right)}^{2} + 2$

$g\left(x\right) = x - \dfrac{1}{x}$

$x \in R - \left\{- 1, 0, 1\right\}$

Let $x - \dfrac{1}{x} = t$

$h\left(x\right) = \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{g\left(x\right)} = \dfrac{{t}^{2} + 2}{t} = t + \dfrac{2}{t}$

$t \in R - \left\{0\right\}$

$h\left(x\right) = t + \dfrac{2}{t}$

$AM \ge GM$

Minimum of $h\left(x\right) ⇒ \dfrac{t + \dfrac{2}{t}}{2} \ge \sqrt{t \times \dfrac{2}{t}}$

$t + \dfrac{2}{t} \ge 2\sqrt{2}$

Local minimum $= 2\sqrt{2}$

questions.q: Twenty meters of wire is available for fencing off a flower-bed in the form of a circular sector. Then the maximum area (in sq. m) of the flower-bed, is:
questions.solution:
Perimeter $= 2r + r\theta = 20$



$\theta = \dfrac{20 - 2r}{r}$

Now, Area $A = \dfrac{{r}^{2}\theta}{2}$

$⇒ A = \dfrac{{r}^{2}}{2}\left(\dfrac{20 - 2r}{r}\right) = 10r - {r}^{2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dA}{dr} = 10 - 2r = 0$

$⇒ r = 5$

$\dfrac{{d}^{2}A}{d{r}^{2}}\left(r = 5\right) = - 2 < 0 ⇒ r = 5$ is the point of maxima

${A}_{max} = 10 \times 5 - 25 = 25$

questions.q: The normal to the curve  $y\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 3\right) = x + 6$ at the point where the curve intersects the $y$-axis passes through the point:
questions.solution:
To find the point where curve intersects the y-axis

Put, $x = 0$, we get

$6y = 6 ⇒ y = 1$

Hence, the point is (0, 1).

On differentiating

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)\left(x - 2\right)\left(x - 3\right) + y\left(2x - 5\right) = 1$

Put, $x = 0, y = 1$, we get

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx}\left(+ 6\right) + 1\left(- 5\right) = 1$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$

$⇒$ Slope of normal $= - 1$

Equation of normal at $\left(0, 1\right)$

$⇒ y - 1 = - 1\left(x - 0\right)$

$⇒ x + y - 1 = 0$

Point $\left(\dfrac{1}{2}, \dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ satisfy the normal.

questions.q: Let C be a curve given by $y\left(x\right) = 1 + \sqrt{4x - 3}$,$x > \dfrac{3}{4}$. If $P$ is a point on C, such that the tangent at $P$ has slope $\dfrac{2}{3}$, then a point through which the normal at $P$ passes, is :
questions.solution:
Given,

$y\left(x\right) = 1 + \sqrt{4x - 3}$

So, $\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{4x - 3}} \times 4 = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒$4x - 3 = 9$

$⇒$x = 3$

So, $y = 4$

Equation of normal at $P\left(3, 4\right)$ is $y - 4 = - \dfrac{3}{2}\left(x - 3\right)$

i.e., $2y - 8 = - 3x + 9$

$⇒$3x + 2y - 17 = 0$

Hence only option $A$ is satisfying the equation.

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right) = \sin^{4} ⁡ x + \cos^{4} ⁡ x .$ Then, $f$ is an increasing function in the interval:
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \sin^{4} ⁡ x + \cos^{4} ⁡ x$

${f}^{′}\left(x\right) = 4\sin^{3} ⁡ xcos ⁡ x + 4\cos^{3} ⁡ x\left(- sin ⁡ x\right)$

$= 4sin ⁡ xcos ⁡ x\left(\sin^{2} ⁡ x - \cos^{2} ⁡ x\right)$

$= - 2sin ⁡ 2xcos ⁡ 2x$

$= - sin ⁡ 4x$

$f\left(x\right)$, is increasing when ${f}^{′}\left(x\right) > 0$

$⇒$- sin ⁡ 4x > 0$

$⇒$sin ⁡ 4x < 0$

$⇒ \pi < 4x < 2\pi$

$⇒ \dfrac{\pi}{4} < x < \dfrac{\pi}{2}$
$⇒$x \in \left(\dfrac{\pi}{4}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

questions.q: The minimum distance of a point on the curve $y = {x}^{2} - 4$ from the origin is
questions.solution:
A variable point on the given parabola can be taken as $\left(\alpha, {\alpha}^{2} - 4\right)$



Distance from origin $D = \sqrt{{\alpha}^{2} + {\left({\alpha}^{2} - 4\right)}^{2}}$

$⇒ {D}^{2} = {\alpha}^{2} + {\alpha}^{4} + 16 - 8{\alpha}^{2}$

$= {\alpha}^{4} - 7{\alpha}^{2} + 16$

$\dfrac{d{D}^{2}}{d\alpha} = 4{\alpha}^{3} - 14\alpha = 0$

$⇒ 2\alpha\left(2{\alpha}^{2} - 7\right) = 0$

$⇒\alpha = 0, \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{2}}, - \sqrt{\dfrac{7}{2}}$



$∴ {D}_{min}^{2}at{\alpha}^{2} = \dfrac{7}{2}$

${D}_{min}^{2} = \dfrac{49}{4} - \dfrac{49}{2} + 16$

$= - \dfrac{49}{4} + 16 = \dfrac{15}{4}$

${D}_{min} = \dfrac{\sqrt{15}}{2}$

questions.q: If the tangent at a point $P$, with parameter $t$, on the curve $x = 4{t}^{2} + 3, y = 8{t}^{3} - 1, t \in R,$ meets the curve again at a point $Q$, then the coordinates of $Q$ are :
questions.solution:
Given $P\left(4{t}^{2} + 3, 8{t}^{3} - 1\right)$

$\dfrac{\dfrac{dy}{dt}}{\dfrac{dx}{dt}} = \dfrac{dy}{dx} = 3t$ (slope of tangent at $P$)

Let $Q = \left(4{\lambda}^{2} + 3, 8{\lambda}^{3} - 1\right)$

Slope of $PQ = 3t$

$\dfrac{8{t}^{3} - 8{\lambda}^{3}}{4{t}^{2} - 4{\lambda}^{2}} = 3t$

$⇒${t}^{2} + t\lambda - 2{\lambda}^{2} = 0$

$\left(t - \lambda\right)\left(t + 2\lambda\right) = 0$

$t = \lambda$ or $\lambda = \dfrac{- t}{2}$

$∴$Q\left[{t}^{2} + 3, - {t}^{3} - 1\right]$

$f\left(x\right) = \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{1 + sin ⁡ x}{1 - sin ⁡ x}}\right), x \in \left(0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$

${f}^{′} ( x ) = \dfrac{1}{1 + \left(\dfrac{1 + sin ⁡ x}{1 - sin ⁡ x}\right)} . \dfrac{1}{2}{\left(\dfrac{1 + sin ⁡ x}{1 - sin ⁡ x}\right)}^{- \dfrac{1}{2}} . \left(\dfrac{cos ⁡ x\left(1 - sin ⁡ x\right) + cos ⁡ \left(1 + sin ⁡ x\right)}{{\left(1 - sin ⁡ x\right)}^{2}}\right)$

at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}$

${f}^{′}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{2}}{2} . \dfrac{1}{2}\left(\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right)\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{\dfrac{1}{4}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Slope of tangent $= \dfrac{1}{2}$

So slope of normal $= - 2$

Also at $x = \dfrac{\pi}{6}, y = \tan^{- 1} ⁡ \sqrt{3} = \dfrac{\pi}{3}$ .

questions.q: A wire of length $2$ units is cut into two parts which are bent respectively to form a square of side $= x$ units and a circle of radius $= r$ units. If the sum of the areas of the square and the circle so formed is minimum, then
questions.solution:
Given that $4x + 2\pir = 2$

i.e., $2x + \pir = 1$

Area $A = {x}^{2} + \pi{r}^{2}$

From (i) and (ii)

$r = \dfrac{1}{\pi + 4}$ .......(iii)

$∴$x = 2r$

questions.q: Let $k$ and $K$ be the minimum and the maximum values of the function $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{0.6}}{1 + {x}^{0.6}}\text{in}\left[0, 1\right]$, respectively, then the ordered pair $( k, K )$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
$f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{0.6}}{1 + {x}^{0.6}}$

${f}^{′}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{0.6{\left(1 + x\right)}^{- 0.4}\left(1 + {x}^{0.6}\right) - 0.6{x}^{0.4}{\left(1 + x\right)}^{0.6}}{{\left(1 + {x}^{0.6}\right)}^{2}}$

$= 0.6{\left(1 + x\right)}^{- 0.4}\dfrac{\left[1 + {x}^{0.6} - {x}^{- 0.4}{\left(1 + x\right)}^{2}\right]}{{\left(1 + {x}^{0.6}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{0.6\left({x}^{0.4} - 1\right)}{{\left(1 + x\right)}^{0.4}{\left(1 + {x}^{0.6}\right)}^{2}}$

Clearly it is always negative in $[ 0, 1 ]$

minimum value would be at $x = 1$.

$\dfrac{{( 1 + 1 )}^{0.6}}{1 + {\left(1\right)}^{0.6}} = \dfrac{{2}^{0.6}}{2} = {2}^{- 0.4} = k$

& maximum values would be at $x = 0$

$\dfrac{{( 1 + 0 )}^{0.6}}{1 + {\left(0\right)}^{0.6}} = \dfrac{1}{1} = K$

Hence $\left({2}^{- 0.4}, 1\right)$

questions.q: If Rolle's theorem holds for the function $f\left(x\right) = 2{x}^{3} + b{x}^{2} + cx, x \in \left[- 1, 1\right]$ at the point $x = \dfrac{1}{2},$ then $2b + c$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Since, Rolle's theorem is satisfied in $[ - 1, 1 ]$ and corresponding to $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$ we have $f ( - 1 ) = f ( 1 )$ & ${f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = 0$

So, $- 2 + b - c = 2 + b + c$

$⇒ c = - 2$

Further ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 6{x}^{2} + 2bx + c$

Put $x = \dfrac{1}{2}$

So ${f}^{'}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{3}{2} + b + c = 0$

$⇒ b = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Hence, $2b + c = - 1$

questions.q: The distance from the origin, of the normal to the curve, $x = 2cos ⁡ t + 2tsin ⁡ t, y = 2sin ⁡ t - 2tcos ⁡ tatt = \dfrac{\pi}{4},$ is :
questions.solution:
At $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4}$,

$x = 2\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} + 2\dfrac{\pi}{4} . \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \left(\sqrt{2} + \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) = \left(\dfrac{4 + \pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$y = 2\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 2\dfrac{\pi}{4} ⋅ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = \left(\sqrt{2} - \dfrac{\pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) = \left(\dfrac{4 - \pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 2cos ⁡ t - 2\left[cos ⁡ t + t ( - sin ⁡ t )\right] = 2tsin ⁡ t$

$\dfrac{dx}{dt} = - 2sin ⁡ t + 2\left[sin ⁡ t + t ⋅ cos ⁡ t\right] = 2tcos ⁡ t$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = tan ⁡ t$ at $t = \dfrac{\pi}{4} ⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = tan ⁡ \dfrac{\pi}{4} = 1$

$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = 1$ .

Slope of tangent is $1$ & therefore slope of normal would be $- 1$.

Equation of normal $y - \left(\dfrac{4 - \pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right) = - 1\left(x - \left(\dfrac{4 + \pi}{2\sqrt{2}}\right)\right)$

questions.q: Let $f\left(x\right)$ be a polynomial of degree four and having its extreme values at $x = 1$ and $x = 2$. If $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$, then $f\left(2\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Let $f\left(x\right) = a{x}^{4} + b{x}^{3} + c{x}^{2} + dx + e$

Then $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + \dfrac{f\left(x\right)}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$

$⇒ \lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + a{x}^{2} + bx + c + \dfrac{d}{x} + \dfrac{e}{{x}^{2}}\right] = 3$

This limit exists when $d = e = 0$.

So, $\lim_{x \to 0}\left[1 + a{x}^{2} + bx + c\right] = 3$

$⇒ c + 1 = 3$

$⇒ c = 2$

It is given, $x = 1$ and $x = 2$ are the solution of ${f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 0$.

$⇒ {f}^{'}\left(x\right) = 4a{x}^{3} + 3b{x}^{2} + 2cx$

$⇒ x\left(4a{x}^{2} + 3bx + 2c\right) = 0$

Given $1, 2$ are the roots of the quadratic equation.

$⇒ \text{Sum of roots} = \dfrac{- 3b}{4a} = 1 + 2 = 3$

$⇒ b = - 4a$

Product of roots $= \dfrac{2c}{4a} = 1 \cdot 2 = 2$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{c}{4}$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{,}b = - 2$

$∴ f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{1}{2}{x}^{4} - 2{x}^{3} + 2{x}^{2}$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = 8 - 16 + 8$

$⇒ f\left(2\right) = 0$

questions.q: If the volume of a spherical ball is increasing at the rate of $4\picc / sec$ then the rate of increase of its radius $\left(incm / sec\right),$ when the volume is $288\picc$ is
questions.solution:
Volume of sphere of radius $r$ is $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3}$

Given $V = 288\picc$

$⇒ 288\pi = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3}$

$⇒ {r}^{3} = 288 \times \dfrac{3}{4} = 216$

$⇒ r = 6cm$.

Again, $V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi{r}^{3}$

Differentiate w.r.t. '$t$'

$⇒ \dfrac{dV}{dt} = 4\pi{r}^{2}\dfrac{dr}{dt}$

Put the given values, to get

$⇒ 4\pi = 4\pi \times {6}^{2} \times \dfrac{dr}{dt}$

$⇒ \dfrac{dr}{dt} = \dfrac{1}{36}cm / sec .$

questions.q: If non-zero real numbers $b and c$ are such that  $minf\left(x\right) > maxg\left(x\right), where $f$\left(x\right)$ = {x}^{2} + 2bx + 2{c}^{2} and g $\left(x\right)$ = - {x}^{2} - 2cx + {b}^{2}, $\left(x \in R\right)$; then $\left|\dfrac{c}{b}\right|$ lies in the interval
questions.solution:
Given& $f\left(x\right) = x^{2} + 2bx + 2c^{2}$ and& $g\left(x\right) = - x^{2} - 2cx + b^{2}$

For finding the minimum value of& $f ( x ) ,$

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 2x + 2b = 0$

$⇒ x = - b$

Also, $f^{"} \left(x\right) = 2$

$⇒ f^{"}\left(-b\right) = 2 > 0$

So, $f\left(x\right)$ has minimum value at& $x = - b$

Hence, ${f}_\min = b^{2} - 2b^{2} + 2c^{2}$

& $⇒ {f}_\min = 2c^{2} - b^{2}$

Similarly, for finding the& maximum value of& $g ( x )$

$g^{'}\left(x\right) = - 2x - 2c = 0$

& & & & & & & & & & $⇒ x = - c$

Also, $g^{"} \left(x\right) = - 2$

$g^{"}\left(-c\right) = - 2 < 0$

So, $g\left(x\right)$ has maximum value at& $x = - c$.

Hence, ${g}_\max = - c^{2} + 2c^{2} + b^{2}$

& $⇒ {g}_\max = c^{2} + b^{2}$

Given ${f}_\min > {g}_\max⇒ 2c^{2} - b^{2} > c^{2} + b^{2}\text{⇒}\left(c^{2} - 2b^{2}\right) > 0$\text{⇒}\left(c - \sqrt{2}b\right)\left(c + \sqrt{2}b\right) > 0$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{c}{b} - \sqrt{2}\right)\left(\dfrac{c}{b} + \sqrt{2}\right) > 0$

Using wavy curve method, we get $\dfrac{c}{b} < - \sqrt{2}$ or& $\dfrac{c}{b} > \sqrt{2}$

$∴ \left|\dfrac{c}{b}\right| \in \left(\sqrt{2}, \infty\right).$

questions.q: For the curve $\mathrm{y}=3 \sin \theta \cos \theta, \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{e}^\theta \sin \theta$, $0 \leq \theta \leq \pi$, the tangent is parallel to $\mathrm{x}$-axis when $\theta$ is:
questions.solution:
Given, $y=3 \sin \theta \cdot \cos \theta \begin{aligned}$&$\frac{d y}{d \theta}=$3[\sin $\theta(-\sin \theta)+\cos \theta(\cos \theta)]$\\
&$\frac{d y}{d \theta}=$3$\left[\cos ^$2 $\theta-\sin ^$2 $\theta\right]=$3 \cos 2 $\theta .$\\
&$\text{$ and }x=$\mathrm{e}^\theta \sin \theta$\\
&$\frac{d x}{d \theta}=$e^$\theta \cos \theta+\sin \theta$e^$\theta$\\
&$\frac{d x}{d \theta}=$e^$\theta(\sin \theta+\cos \theta)
\end{aligned}$Dividing (1) by (2)

$\begin{gathered}\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{3 \cos 2 \theta}{e^\theta(\sin \theta+\cos \theta)}=\frac{3\left(\cos ^2 \theta-\sin ^2 \theta\right)}{e^\theta(\sin \theta+\cos \theta)}$\\
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{3(\cos \theta+\sin \theta)(\cos \theta-\sin \theta)}{e^\theta(\sin \theta+\cos \theta)}$\\
$\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{3(\cos \theta-\sin \theta)}{e^\theta}
\end{gathered}$Given tangent is parallel to $x$-axis then
$\frac{d y}{d x}=00=\frac{3(\cos \theta-\sin \theta)}{e^\theta}$ or $\cos \theta-\sin \theta=0 \Rightarrow \cos \theta=\sin \theta\Rightarrow \tan \theta=1 \Rightarrow \tan \theta=\frac{\tan \pi}{4} \Rightarrow \theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$

$∴ {f}^{'}$\left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$ = 0 ⇒ 6 \times $\dfrac{1}{4} +$2a \times $\dfrac{1}{2} +$b = 0$

$⇒ a = $\dfrac{1}{2}

$⇒ 2a + b = - 1$

Adding,

$∴ \alpha = 2$

questions.q: The slope of the line touching both the parabolas ${y}^{2} = 4x$ and ${x}^{2} = - 32y$ is
questions.solution:
${y}^{2} = 4\left(1\right)x$

${x}^{2} = 4\left(- 8\right)y$

The equation of the tangent to ${y}^{2} = 4x$ is $y = mx + \dfrac{a}{m}$
The equation of the tangent to ${x}^{2} = 4by$ is $y = mx - b{m}^{2}$

Since, they have a common tangent,

$\dfrac{a}{m} = - b{m}^{2}$

$∴ \dfrac{1}{m} = 8{m}^{2}$

$∴ {m}^{3} = \dfrac{1}{8}$

$∴ m = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴$ The slope of the common tangent is $\dfrac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: Let $f(1)=-2$ and $f^{\prime}(x) \geq 4.2$ for $1 \leq x \leq 6$. The possible value of $f(6)$ lies in the interval :
questions.solution:
Given $f(1)=-2$ and $f^{\prime}(x) \geq 4.2$ for $1 \leq x \leq 6$
Consider $f^{\prime}(x)=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$\Rightarrow f(x+h)-f(x)=f^{\prime}(x) \cdot h \geq(4.2) h$
So, $f(x+h) \geq f(x)+(4.2) h$
put $x=1$ and $h=5$, we get
$f(6) \geq f(1)+5(4.2) \Rightarrow f(6) \geq 19$
Hence $f(6)$ lies in $[19, \infty)$

questions.q: If an equation of a tangent to the curve, $y-\cos (x+f),-1-1 \leq x \leq 1+\pi$, is $x+2 y=k$ then $k$ is equal to :
questions.solution:
Let $y=\cos (x+y) ⇒ \frac{d y}{d x}=-\sin ($x+y)$\left($1+$\frac{d y}{d x}\right)$Now, given equation of tangent is

$\begin{aligned}$&x+2 y=k \\
&\Rightarrow $\text{ Slope }=\frac{-1}{2}
\end{aligned}$So, $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-1}{2}$ put this value in (1), we get

$\begin{aligned}$&$\frac{-1}{2}=-\sin ($x+y)$\left($1-$\frac{1}{2}\right)$\\
&\Rightarrow \sin (x+y)=1 \\
&\Rightarrow x+y=$\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow$y=$\frac{\pi}{2}-$x
\end{aligned}

Now $\frac{\pi}{2}-x=\cos (x+y)$
\Rightarrow x=$\frac{\pi}{2} \text{ and }$y=0

Thus $x+2 y=k \quad \Rightarrow \frac{\pi}{2}=k$

 \begin{aligned}
&x+2 y=k \\
&\Rightarrow $\text{ Slope }=$\frac{-1}{2}$
\end{aligned} 
So, $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-1}{2}$ put this value in (1), we get
 \begin{aligned}
&\frac{-1}{2}=-\sin (x+y)\left(1-\frac{1}{2}\right) \\
&\Rightarrow \sin (x+y)=1 \\
&\Rightarrow x+y=\frac{\pi}{2} \Rightarrow y=\frac{\pi}{2}-x
\end{aligned} 
Now $\frac{\pi}{2}-$x=$\cos$(x+y) $
\Rightarrow x=\frac{\pi}{2} \text{ and } y=0
 
Thus $x+2 y=k \quad \Rightarrow $\frac{\pi}{2}=$k

questions.q: The maximum area of a right angled triangle with hypotenuse $h$ is :
questions.solution:
Let base $=b$
Altitude (or perpendicular) $=\sqrt{h^2-b^2}$ Area, $\mathrm{A}=\frac{1}{2} \times$ base $\times$ altitude $=\frac{1}{2} \times b \times \sqrt{h^2-b^2}$\Rightarrow \frac{d \mathrm{~A}}{d b}=\frac{1}{2}\left[\sqrt{h^2-b^2}+b \cdot \frac{-2 b}{2 \sqrt{h^2-b^2}}\right]$=\frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{h^2-2 b^2}{\sqrt{h^2-b^2}}\right]$ Put $\frac{d \mathrm{~A}}{d b}=0, \Rightarrow b=\frac{h}{\sqrt{2}}$ Maximumarea $=\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{h}{\sqrt{2}} \times \sqrt{h^2-\frac{h^2}{2}}=\frac{h^2}{4}$

& \Rightarrow 8=8 $\pi$r $\frac{d r}{d t} \Rightarrow \frac{d r}{d t}=\frac{1}{\pi r}

questions.q: The normal to the curve $x=a(\cos \theta+\theta \sin \theta), y=a(\sin \theta-\theta \cos \theta)$ at any point ' $\theta$ ' is such that
options:
it passes through the origin

it makes angle $\frac{\pi}{2}+\theta$ with the $x$-axis

it passes through $\left(\mathrm{a} \frac{\pi}{2},-\mathrm{a}\right)$

it is at a constant distance from the origin
questions.solution:
Clearly $\frac{\mathrm{dy}}{\mathrm{dx}}=\tan \theta \Rightarrow$ slope of normal $=-\cot \theta$
Equation of normal at ' $\theta$ ' is
$y-a(\sin \theta-\theta \cos \theta)=-\cot \theta(x-a(\cos \theta+\theta \sin \theta)$\Rightarrow y \sin \theta-a \sin ^2 \theta+a \theta \cos \theta \sin \theta=-x \cos \theta+a \cos ^2 \theta+a \theta \sin \theta \cos \theta$\Rightarrow x \cos \theta+y \sin \theta=a$
Clearly this is an equation of straight line which is at a constant distance 'a' from origin.

questions.q: If $f$ is a real-valued differentiable function satisfying $|f(x)-f(y)| \leq(x-y)^2, x, y \in R$ and $f(0)=0$, then $f(1)$ equals
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$& f^{\prime}(x)=$\lim _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$\\
& $\left|$f^{\prime}(x)\right|=$\lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left|\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}\right| \leq \lim _{h \rightarrow 0}\left|\frac{(h)^2}{h}\right|$\\
& \Rightarrow$\left|$f^{\prime}(x)\right| \leq 0 \Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)=0 \quad \Rightarrow f(x)=$\text{ constant }$\\
& $\text{ As }$f(0)=0 \Rightarrow f(1)=0 .
\end{aligned}
